articles.title: The world’s first foldable phone is charmingly awful
articles.summary: The Royole FlexPai is officially the world’s first foldable phone, but its maker has achieved the feat by rushing the device out to market way before it’s ready for prime time. The threat of Samsung and Huawei stealing the small Chinese company’s thunder was simply too much to resist, and that’s how we ended up with the unfinished, unpolished FlexPai on exhibit at CES 2019.
articles.body: The Royole FlexPai is the sort of device that companies rush out when they feel the absolute imperative to be first with some new technology. I don’t blame Royole — a five-year-old company literally founded for the purpose of developing and selling flexible displays — because it faced the existential threat of Samsung coming in and stealing its thunder with a rival foldable device. So Royole hurriedly threw the FlexPai together and let the world gawk at its wondrous, foldable awfulness. I got to grips with the FlexPai today and I was amused by how dysfunctional most of its software was. But let’s talk hardware first. Measuring 7.8 inches diagonally, this is an Android tablet in its extended mode which becomes two, not just one, Android phones when it’s flexed closed. Yes, Royole is apparently a hyper-ambitious company. It provides two SIM slots and tries to provide an auto-detection system that only shows content on the half of the folded screen that you’re facing at any given time. One of the two phones is assigned as the primary, and its content spills out onto the full tablet when the device is opened. [Image: You get a 1920 x 1440 resolution on the full display, which shrinks to less than half when you’re in phone mode, thanks in large part to the huge swath of disused OLED screen that wraps around the wide-arcing hinge. Still, a 308ppi pixel density is sufficient for the screen to look reasonably sharp. The bigger issue with it is that it’s simply of poor quality. In my 40 minutes with the FlexPai, I noticed color banding, weird dim areas right in the middle of the screen, and the sort of hyper-saturation that was characteristic of Samsung’s first and second-generation AMOLED screens from many years ago. Royole has done a good job of making the FlexPai robust. I initially feared I would break it when approaching the fully folded position, but that’s when it just snaps cleanly into a stiff, closed form. It actually requires a fair amount of force from the user to open and close it, which gives me a reassuring sense that it can withstand rough handling. A substantial cause for my reluctance to get too hyped up about foldables is the preconception that they’d be even more fragile than modern-day smartphones. But the Royole FlexPai seems to have been engineered well enough to dispute that notion. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The biggest failure of the FlexPai is, predictably, its software and basic operation. Any time you rotate the device or fold / unfold it, it gets deeply confused and freaked out. I saw apps stacking on top of each other and overlapping with widgets as the tablet was transitioning into phone mode. I launched the camera accidentally more than once. There’s nothing intuitive about the automatic switch between the two phones. Royole’s software is called Water OS, and I definitely felt out of my depth. Logic and predictability are at a premium anytime you pick this device up. Lest you think the Royole FlexPai is some sort of distant-future concept, you should know that it’s already on sale in China for 8,999 yuan. That equates to roughly $1,320 in US currency, and Royole would happily sell you a developer edition for the same price over here in the States if you’re into the sort of awkward, goofy weirdness this folding tablet provides. articles.title: Logitech’s Lift is a low-cost vertical mouse that might convert you
articles.summary: Logitech’s new Lift wireless vertical mouse has many of the same features as the pricier MX Vertical but with a more simplified design and a lower price. It runs on a single AA, which Logitech claims can last for up to two years.
articles.body: Logitech has announced Lift, a $69.99 wireless vertical mouse that’s available starting today in multiple colorways, as well as with both right- and left-handed options. The Lift features a vertically oriented design that puts your hand at a 57-degree angle for better ergonomics. Compared to using a traditional mouse, using mice like the Lift may help to greatly reduce wrist strain since you’re holding your wrist at a similar angle to shaking someone’s hand. At least, that’s what I experienced. Last year, I made the shift to a split ergonomic keyboard, and a mouse like the Lift completes the setup. For those keeping track, the Lift isn’t quite as fully featured as the pricier $99.99 MX Vertical, but it could be a good starting option if you don’t want to spend that much. It lacks USB-C charging, instead running off of a single AA battery that Logitech claims can (impressively) last up to two years. [Media: The Lift ditches the elegant design of the MX Vertical for something that’s more simplified and playful (plus, you can get it in graphite, silver, or pink). It retains the rubber grip to keep it snug in your palm, and most of the same key functionality is here. The mouse has two main buttons, a scroll wheel that emphasizes smooth, quiet scrolling, a DPI switching button, and two thumb buttons. On its bottom, there’s a button for toggling between one of three devices that you can connect the Lift to (holding it doubles as the Bluetooth pairing button). [Image: This mouse supports Logitech Flow, the company’s unique software feature that allows the mouse to be used simultaneously on multiple computers — even if they run a different OS. You’ll need the Logi Options Plus app running on both computers; then, the cursor can travel from one PC to the other. The app can also be used to easily copy and paste files between machines. I’ve seen a hands-on demo of this software working, but it just wouldn’t cooperate with me at home. Logitech includes its new Bolt USB receiver with the Lift for quickly connecting to a PC that has a USB-A port. Compared to its previous unifying receiver, this one boasts better security. Or, you can utilize its Bluetooth function, which doesn’t require using a receiver. I’ve had just a couple of days alone with the Lift as my primary mouse, but the transition from a standard mouse has gone smoother than I anticipated. Aside from accidentally knocking my hand into the Lift and tipping it over (it’s much taller than your average mouse), the learning curve isn’t too bad since this mouse has a similar button layout to mice that I’m accustomed to using. If you’ve been curious about vertical mice, the Lift could be a good option to start with since it costs well under $100. [Image: The Lift is very comfortable to use, thanks in part to the rubberized grip.

articles.title: Microsoft is bringing a built-in network speed test to Windows 11
articles.summary: Microsoft is testing a Windows 11 update that adds a network speed test tool to the taskbar.
articles.body: Microsoft is working on a bunch of new features for Windows 11, including a new network speed test that you can access from your taskbar. The tool is bundled in an update rolling out to Windows 11 Insiders in the Release Preview Channel, allowing you to right-click the network icon in the system tray to access a speed test option that opens in your default browser. From there, you can check how fast your connection is over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, or cellular data. Microsoft first started testing this feature last year, and it could offer a convenient alternative to checking your connection speed by navigating to third-party websites. There’s also a new camera settings option coming to the Settings menu, giving you the ability to control the pan and tilt for supported cameras (though Microsoft doesn’t say which devices work with the new feature). Microsoft is adding new emoji to Windows 11, too, a full-page Widget settings menu, and the ability to set .webp files as your desktop background. You can check out the update via the Release Preview Channel. It’s rolling out now to Windows 11 versions 24H2 (Build 26100) and 25H2 (Build 26200).

articles.title: Logitech’s new Mobi Fold squeezes a lot of functionality into a tiny folding mouse
articles.summary: Logitech’s new Mobi Fold is a compact travel mouse that manages to get even smaller by folding in half without skimping on features.
articles.body: Logitech finally announced its new ultraportable travel mouse following leaked marketing images that spoiled the surprise last month. As the name implies, the Mobi Fold is a compact mouse that can fold in half using a hinge that can pivot about 130 degrees. At $79.99 in graphite, off-white, lilac, and sand color options, the Mobi Fold isn’t Logitech’s lightest or cheapest mouse, but it’s definitely one of its smallest and a well-featured alternative to your laptop’s trackpad if you can get used to some unconventional ergonomics. The arch-shaped Mobi Fold looks similar to other folding devices, like the Surface Arc mouse. But while Microsoft’s design folds flat, making it thinner and easier to slip into a pocket or bag, the Mobi Fold is more like a clamshell cellphone. And even though it doesn’t snap shut with a satisfying clunk, it feels durable. Logitech says the hinge was “tested to withstand 15 years of daily use.” [Image: [Image: That hinge, along with more than half the mouse, is wrapped in a silicone skin that improves grip while semi-protecting it from drops. Where it covers the hinge you’ll find a pleated design that expands and stretches when the mouse is folded in half, so there’s no risk of pinching. At 79 grams the Mobi Fold is a few grams heavier than Logitech’s Pebble Mouse 2 and the bare-bones M196 that I’ve been recently traveling with. When folded, the mouse is a little over three-quarters of an inch tall and about 2.6x2.5 inches in size, making it feel seriously compact. It reminds me of some wireless earbud cases, but a bit thinner. [Image: [Image: Logitech claims the Mobi Fold’s rechargeable battery will power the mouse for up to one month on a full charge, while a 1-minute quick charge will keep it going for up to 22 hours. It’s getting a global release. which means we can probably thank recent EU regulations for a removable cover on the underside allowing that rechargeable battery to be replaced in the future. [Product: Logitech Mobi Fold mouse | The Mobi Fold isn’t designed to entirely replace a full-featured desktop mouse, but it offers enough functionality and customizability to be a solid trackpad alternative. There’s a 4K DPI optical sensor on the bottom and a pair of left and right mouse buttons on top with a multifunction touch panel between them. That panel’s behavior can be changed using the optional Logi Options Plus software, so swiping your finger up and down either causes websites and documents to zip by or a more leisurely line by line scroll. The top and bottom of the touch panel also function as two additional clicky buttons. You can customize their functionality using Logitech’s app, but by default they function as forward and back buttons while browsing. [Image: When folded in half, the Mobi Fold is much smaller than the Logitech M196 mouse I frequently travel with, but it trades a scroll wheel for a touch panel. A single button on the underside of the Mobi Fold is used to connect and cycle the mouse between up to three different devices, and I had no difficulty connecting it to a couple of laptops and an iPad. Instead of a dedicated power button, you turn the mouse off by folding it in half. I found that while scrolling with the touch panel remains active when you’ve picked up the mouse to fold it, all of the buttons are disabled. That should prevent accidental presses and clicks because you’ll absolutely be pressing them as you fold it. If portability is your ultimate priority, the Mobi Fold is an excellent way to keep a mouse on hand. You’ll just want to take some extra time to get comfortable using it. [Image: [Image: While Microsoft’s aptly named Arc mouse features a gracefully curved arch that contours to your hand, the Mobi Fold feels more like you’re resting your hands on two sides of a piece of cardboard that’s been folded in half. Its buttons and touch panel are also completely flat, and I’ve come to realize I’m a mouse user who prefers to frequently lift and reposition a mouse instead of moving my entire arm to push it around. The Mobi Fold’s thin design made it hard to do that as I struggled to find a sturdy place to grip it on either side. [Image: If you like to pack light when traveling but want an alternative to your laptop’s trackpad, the Mobi Fold is impressively small but well featured. For $80, the Mobi Fold delivers an impressively portable mouse that also offers more than just basic functionality. I will always choose a physical wheel over a touch pad for scrolling, but I’d happily endure finger swipes given how small this mouse folds up. While I’d still opt for my laptop’s touchpad, the Mobi Fold is an excellent accessory for taking advantage of the iPad’s recent multitasking upgrades. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

articles.title: Gen Z loves read receipts, until someone leaves them on read
articles.summary: Do you get annoyed when you're left on read? Turns out, Gen Z is the most likely to take offense to this social faux pas.
articles.body:
Let's face it: read receipts on texts can be a bit of a minefield. Some people always have them on, others prefer to leave them off for everyone, and being "left on read" — reading someone's text and not responding — is the social faux pas of our time. Some of us are a little more sensitive to it than others, though, and it seems to break down by what generational cohort you fall into, according to a new survey of 2,013 American adults conducted by the Harris Poll for AT&T.

"Over half (56%) of Gen Z Americans (ages 18-29) say they usually keep read receipts turned on for everyone, while 28% of Gen Zers turn read receipts on and off depending on who they're talking to," the survey, which was conducted between Sept. 14-15, says. That's compared to 50% of all respondents who say they keep read receipts on for everyone, while 26% keep them off entirely and 23% turn them on and off depending on who they're talking to.

As you might expect, Gen Z Americans are also the most likely to be annoyed if you read their message and don't respond. A full 48% of Gen Z respondents said they consider being "left on read" to be one of the most annoying things in life, compared to just 22% of baby boomers. For respondents overall, 35% are annoyed with being left on read.

One thing we can all agree on, however, is how annoying it is to lose your Wi-Fi connection when you really need one. The survey found 65% of Americans say losing Wi-Fi at a critical moment is one of the most annoying things in life, followed by being transferred by customer service multiple times (63%) and automated responses that don't answer your questions (60%). The only other answer that topped 50% was having a flight canceled, which 51% of respondents cited.

Interestingly, as impatient as Gen Z may be with read receipts, they're more willing than other generations to give customer service more leeway. When asked whether they'd wait more than 15 minutes for customer service, 36% of Gen Z said yes, while only 22% of Gen X and 13% of boomers said the same. Overall, 76% of respondents said they'd only be willing to wait 15 minutes or less for customer service, with 19% saying they'd be willing to wait less than five minutes.

Of course, as with all sponsored surveys, it's worth taking these results with a grain of salt. The survey was conducted as part of AT&T's "America's Best Guarantee," which promises that customers who call the company will get an answer in five minutes or less. If they don't, they can schedule a call back "at a time they choose." If the company fails on either of those promises, it guarantees a "benefit" for the customer, though it doesn't specify what that benefit is.

Still, if you're worried that you might be a little too impatient at times, it's comforting to know you're definitely not alone.

images.caption: A new survey conducted by The Harris Poll on behalf of AT&T offers some fascinating insights into American phone culture. (Matt Cardy via Getty Images)

articles.title: 'Heated Rivalry' made hockey hot. But some fans say the sport's culture is leaving them out in the cold.
articles.summary: "Heated Rivalry" has sparked a hockey mania. But as fans rush to rinks, they also see opportunities for more inclusion.
articles.body:
Growing up in the icy tundra winters of Ontario, my dad would drag the family out to an Ottawa Senators hockey game at least once a year. I remember the excitement of putting on my jersey and the thunderous cheers after our home team scored. But it became harder to engage with hockey as an adult. Maybe it's because watching rambunctious players pick a fight with each other on ice no longer felt entertaining; more likely it's because I'm queer and didn't see myself in hockey culture. Then came Heated Rivalry .

For those who haven't yet indulged, Heated Rivalry primarily follows the story of two hockey players, Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams), a Canadian player for the fictional Montreal Metros, and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie), a Russian player for the Boston Raiders. They are pitted against each other by hockey media and fans as star captains on rival teams, but eventually realize they also have irresistible chemistry — leading to years of no-strings-attached hookups until they finally face the depths of their feelings for each other.

When the Canadian series debuted last November, buzzing with both the sensationalism of the graphic sex scenes and the tenderness of a queer love story , it sparked a sort of hockey mania, with fans of the show flocking to "boy aquariums." The Heated Rivalry effect has given rise to an entirely new subset of hockey enthusiasts, as confirmed by various sources reporting an increase in first-time NHL ticket buyers. It made me rethink my relationship with the sport: Could it be for me too?

But there has been one common thread — particularly among women and queer fans, some of whom I interviewed for this piece: the moral conflict of balancing their love for the fast-paced, dynamic sport with the NHL — the real-life professional hockey league, as opposed to the "Major League Hockey" featured in the show — and its inability to fully lean into the Heated Rivalry of it all. Heated Rivalry creator Jacob Tierney pushed back in a recent viral clip from Andy Cohen's podcast after Cohen suggested the league had "met the moment."

Tierney specifically called out the league's reinstatement of five former Hockey Canada players after they were acquitted of sexual assault charges last year. For critics, it's just the latest example of toxicity within the broader hockey culture .

Rachel Reid, the author of the Game Changers books on which the TV series is based, says she's felt "bad" about being a hockey fan over the years. "It's so homophobic and awful, and misogynist ; there are so many reasons not to be a fan," Reid said at a recent event for WBUR CitySpace . She included a searing subplot in the series that is critical of the NHL, and a sexual assault storyline that some fans speculate will play out in the show's upcoming second season, set for release next spring.

And yet, for fans, Heated Rivalry still inspires them to immerse themselves in the sport. Amy Chen in Boston has rewatched Heated Rivalry repeatedly since the six episodes first streamed on HBO Max, and it wasn't long until hockey IRL became an area of interest as well. Chen says the timing of the Winter Olympics was the catalyst that led her to pay closer attention to the NHL. She's a huge Bruins fan now, but came into it completely fresh: "I didn't know what a face-off was, I didn't know what the boards were. It's kind of awesome that they hit each other and it's allowed."

That being said, Chen has been navigating what she calls the "cognitive dissonance" of being a hockey fan in 2026. "A lot of fans feel conflicted about supporting their teams while also implicitly supporting the league as an organization," she says. "If they actually did something meaningful to address it, I think a lot of people would feel better about being hockey fans."

Speaking to reporters in January, NHL commissioner Gary Bettman called Heated Rivalry a "wonderful story" that is driving more people to watch games in person. "The content, particularly for young people, may be a little spicy. And so you have to balance that out in terms of how you embrace it," he said.

Since then, there have been minor brushes with the series — such as the NHL's release of hockey romance audio stories that are no longer available on Spotify after negative fan reception, or songs from the Heated Rivalry soundtrack playing at games. But these gestures feel "performative" to fans like Chen.

Cayla Sacre, an L.A.-based fan of the Kings, says she loves watching an arena come alive when a song from the Heated Rivalry soundtrack plays during intermission, easily highlighting who in attendance is a fan of the show as they sing along to Feist or t.A.T.u. She also says it's been much easier to get a group of girlfriends together for a night out at a hockey game. "I literally took a group of five queer women to a Kings game," she says. "We had a great time, but that would never have happened a year ago."

To Sacre, it's in the NHL's interest to do more to actively welcome more women and queer people at games. Embracing Heated Rivalry would be an important first step. "The more you do that, the more they're going to see those numbers sticking around, and the louder of a noise we can make," she says. "It's better for all people if you can promote the diversity within your sport and make it a safe space."

Sacre tells me she's noticed some events aimed at diversifying the fan base, such as Pride Nights and a celebration of Hispanic Heritage Month , but she wonders about bigger systemic changes. "Is there actually anything happening in the sport itself?" she wonders.

Steven Mata, based in Austin, sometimes drives over to Dallas to watch the Stars play and keeps up more religiously with the Detroit Red Wings. He couldn't find any NHL-related Heated Rivalry events but did attend one with the Boston Red Sox [Ilya plays for the fictional Boston Raiders] — promoted by the MLB . "It was massive," he tells me. "Like crazy, insane lines, people spent so much money — there was all this merch and photo ops." Reid even made a surprise appearance to throw out the first pitch, delighting fans.

On the NHL side of things, the Dallas Stars canceled their Pride Night for the first time in five years. (In a statement, a team spokesperson shared that the event hosted in its place, "Hockey Unites Night: Women in Sports," would allow "our organization to use our platform to celebrate and support a different underrepresented community each season.") "At the end of the day, capitalism is always going to win," Mata says. "So you would think, Oh, here's this opportunity, but they just haven't leaned in."

Over in Canada, the Toronto Gay Hockey Association (TGHA), one of the oldest queer hockey recreational leagues in the world, has seen an increase in registrations since Heated Rivalry . They currently organize 20 teams with over 150 hopeful players on the waitlist from their recent registration cycle.

Ben Baby, the league's commissioner who has played hockey for the last decade or so, says the league has a "really strong" relationship with the NHL, which selected Toronto to host the inaugural Pride Cup in 2024 as part of the NHL Unites program. It's also where NHL commissioner Bettman presented the league with a $25,000 check. "They have been good to us at a league level," Baby says. "I've seen some good stuff behind the scenes."

It's in the public arena where issues arise. Over the years, the TGHA's relationship with the NHL has given them an opportunity to voice their concerns when necessary, especially regarding the 2023 banning of hockey-stick Pride Tape and the policy shift on players wearing Pride jerseys . "How much of it is heard is unknown, but we are able to reach out and use that channel to advocate for what we believe or what we know to be right," Baby says.

Baby points out there's a distinction between how individual teams, or "franchises," might decide to take advantage of the Heated Rivalry wave, which many of them have — while it's higher levels at the NHL that are taking longer to adapt and implement a more inclusive environment. "It's unfortunate because they could be seizing the moment and really running with it, but we don't see that," he says.

And if the NHL never evolves? I received numerous messages from fans who have floated over to the Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL) instead, or other sports where they feel more welcome. Baby says it's a great time for would-be fans to stop by a local rec league to see what inclusive hockey could really look like. He invites all to the stands of the Mattamy Athletic Centre in Toronto on Sunday afternoons to watch queer hockey players dominate the ice.

For the fans I spoke with who are willing to stick it out with the NHL, there is a shared hope that Heated Rivalry is the push the league needs to move in the right direction, even if that progress is slow. It's worth noting that the current NHL season is just a few weeks old, and one that has seen teams — or their social media channels, anyway — catch up to trends like tunnel fits (no longer bound to a restrictive dress code) and opening night arrivals . If the NHL is willing to part with decades-old restrictions on players' personal fashion expression, what other changes might they be looking to embrace going forward?

"Is it the NHL's job to be an advocate for inclusion? You know, I wish it was. In sports, hockey is one of the last vestiges and the slowest ones for the culture to change." Baby says. "Let inclusion become a part of the game. Let's keep taking steps forward, at minimum. Let's not take steps back."

articles.title: Our best tips for using the iPhone Duo
articles.summary: The iPhone Duo encourages you to use it in lots of new ways, which comes with a learning curve. Here are some tips to get you started.
articles.body: The Duo is an entirely new kind of iPhone, so it comes with a bit of a learning curve. That’s a wild thing to imagine, since the iPhone has had very few fundamental changes since its inception. But the Duo is built different. If you won the preorder lottery and managed to get your hands on one today, you’ll see what that means. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll lose track of the volume buttons as you turn the thing around. We’ve learned a few tricks over the past week of flipping and folding the Duo as much as we could. Here are our favorite tips and hacks for newly minted Duo owners. You can set orientation lock on each screen independently I learned this one when someone on Threads asked about it. Normally, I keep screen orientation lock enabled because I hate it when everything flips unintentionally. But the Duo is built to be used in different orientations. So, throughout my first week with the phone, I just left it unlocked and didn’t think twice about it. But it turns out that if you lock orientation on the outer screen to preserve your sanity, you can leave it unlocked for the inner screen, which you are much more likely to want to rotate. And even with orientation locked on the cover screen, videos will still rotate automatically if you prop it up in tent mode. [Image: [Image: You can automatically remap the volume buttons to match orientation The iPhone Duo is a phone that you sometimes end up using upside down. It happened to us a lot; you flip open the screen, and for some reason it feels natural to rotate the screen clockwise. But this orients the volume controls so that the bottom button turns the volume up and the top one turns it down. You can change this setting. Go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Fixed Position Volume Controls and toggle it off. Now, when you rotate the inner screen clockwise, you’ll press the top button to increase the volume. Why isn’t this the default behavior? Great question. You can tap the Wi-Fi status icon to bring up Control Center Now that Apple has three shortcuts mapped to swipes from the top of the iPhone screen — swipe from the top left for notifications, the middle for Siri, and the top right for Control Center — it’s easy to miss whatever you were going for on the first try. All three shortcuts appear on the Duo as well, but there’s another way to pull up the Control Center — just tap the new, unified Wi-Fi / battery status icon. This will fully reveal the Control Center and expand the status icon into its independent parts. It’s a small thing, but anything that makes the phone easier to use one-handed is welcome in my book. [Image: [Image: You should register a bunch of fingers with Touch ID You might be tempted to speed through setup and just register one finger for Touch ID, but it’s worth doing a few more while you’re at it. Once again, the Duo is a phone you’re going to flip around and reorient by its nature. So while your right-hand thumb makes sense for unlocking the cover screen, it requires an awkward maneuver to use that finger once you’ve opened the phone and rotated it. Your left-hand index finger will be closer to the Touch ID sensor if you rotate the phone counterclockwise the way Apple CEO John Ternus seemingly intended. And it sounds silly, but enrolling your right-hand pinky is a good move for those occasions when you turn the inner screen clockwise. You can watch a video and open an app below it in portrait orientation, but it’s complicated The iPhone Duo very much only wants you to multitask with two apps side by side in landscape mode using the inner screen. There’s no window resizing, no additional apps. And if you turn the phone to portrait orientation, one of those apps flies away and you’re down to one. But there is technically a way to get two apps going in this orientation — it’s just wonky. [Image: Start playing a video in an app like Prime Video, then tap the picture-in-picture (PiP) icon to move it to a PiP window. Swipe away to get to the homescreen, open another app, then rotate the phone to portrait. An icon to stack the video on top of the open app will appear in the PiP window. You might want a PopSocket I picked up a PopSocket habit while using the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold, and it makes a tremendous difference when you’re holding such a heavy phone for a long time. It’s especially appealing on the Pro Fold and the Duo because they both have magnets built into the back panel. You can thwack it onto the phone when you want it and just take it off when you don’t. The MagSafe PopSocket I’ve been using with the Duo has been more than strong enough to support the phone’s weight. If you’re picking up a Duo today and discover a neat trick as you use your new phone, drop it in the comments below. We’re all learning together here.

articles.title: The Sigma FP2 brings significant upgrades to the ‘world’s smallest’ full-frame camera
articles.summary: Sigma’s first follow-up to its seven-year-old fp full-frame camera, the FP2 comes with a long list of upgrades and improvements.
articles.body: Seven years after Sigma claimed its original fp was the world’s smallest and lightest full-frame mirrorless camera, the company has announced a similarly compact follow-up with several welcome upgrades, including an improved sensor, an articulating LCD display, and longer battery life. But this time around, Sigma is only claiming its new FP2 is the “world’s smallest” full-frame shooter since those upgrades have increased its body-only weight by about 6 grams. The Sigma FP2 will be available on November 11th and starts at $2,199 for the camera body alone. For $2,749, you can bundle it with Sigma’s upgraded EVF-21 viewfinder featuring a 5.76 million dot OLED panel and an eye sensor the camera uses to switch between its LCD screen and viewfinder. For the same price, you can alternately bundle the new camera with an I-series 50mm F2 DG lens. [Image: The FP2’s sensor upgrades don’t include more resolution but provide faster data speeds to facilitate higher shooter rates and new autofocus capabilities. The biggest upgrade for the FP2 is a new 24.5-megapixel, partially stacked, back-side illuminated, full-frame CMOS sensor. In terms of resolution, it’s a tiny step down from the original fp’s 24.6-megapixel sensor, but the new architecture allows for faster data reading off the FP2’s sensor. That comes with many benefits, including a reduced rolling shutter effect in stills (the camera is still limited to just an electronic shutter), faster autofocus capabilities that now include bird recognition in addition to people and animals, still shooting at up to 20fps, and video capabilities that max out at 6K at 60fps, or 4K at 120fps when using only a cropped portion of the sensor. [Image: The FP2’s new articulated screen can tilt up and down and extends away from the camera’s body to improve cooling when recording video. The Sigma FP2 carries forward the streamlined and compact body of the original which can still occasionally result in challenging ergonomics, particularly with a longer lens attached. But multiple tripod mounts facilitate the use of optional accessories, like an extended grip and the aforementioned viewfinder. Its 3.2-inch, 2.1 million dot LCD touchscreen on the back can now angle up and down to facilitate more shooting angles while at the same time improving airflow and cooling so the FP2 can record longer videos. Sigma added a full-size HDMI port, which is more durable than the original fp’s micro HDMI option, alongside two USB-C ports. One is limited to USB 2.0 speeds and is primarily designed to be used for powering the camera or connecting accessories like headphones or the viewfinder. The other is a 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 port that can be used for high-speed data transfers or for connecting an external SSD for capturing footage in Apple’s ProRes RAW format. There’s just a single SD card slot, so there’s no option for redundant backup storage, but the FP2 does come with 70GB of storage built-in that can be used when your memory card unexpectedly fills up. Sigma has also increased the capacity of the battery in the FP2. It makes the new model closer to 40 grams heavier than the original fp with the battery inserted but offers 30 percent longer battery life, which equates to around 370 photos, or about 130 minutes of video capture, according to the company.

articles.title: Texas football knows what it expects. Does it know what it needs?
articles.summary: Texas won at least 10 games nine straight years under Mack Brown and four times in the 12 seasons since. Brown’s best years hold a lesson for Steve Sarkisian...
articles.body:
In January 2013, Mack Brown was still the head coach at Texas, coming off a nine-win season . A regent and a former regent were already on the phone with Nick Saban's agent .

Saban stayed at Alabama. News of his contract extension broke that December, minutes before Brown was scheduled to speak at the Texas football banquet, and Brown stepped down the next day . Three weeks later, Texas hired Charlie Strong , a coach it never really wanted in the first place. Red McCombs, whose name is on the business school, ripped the hire on the radio .

Since Brown, Texas has hired a fallback, a cure, and a better version of the cure. Strong, a defensive coach, took over his own defense's play-calling in his third year and never posted a winning record . So Texas swung the other way with Tom Herman, the offensive coordinator for Ohio State's 2014 national champions . When Herman hit a wall, Texas hired more or less the same coach again in Steve Sarkisian: Herman with fancier pre-snap motion, scripted play designs, and a better résumé. He has accomplished more at Texas than either predecessor.

Texas keeps shopping for the hot name or the offensive mind. The job has always been bigger than either. On his way out, Brown passed along how Darrell Royal described it — so many kinds of people follow Texas football that the coach has to pull them all together. Royal compared it to a box of BBs scattered across a room. The coach has to "get all the BBs back in the box."

Royal is the best coach Texas has ever had, and his way isn't coming back. He was his own athletic director for most of his career, and he won with the wishbone, an offense his own staff drew up . Nobody gets that setup again.

Brown's way can come back because it ran on people. He worked the politics and kept the big-money alumni at bay, the ones who want a say without ever having coached a down. He put great position coaches around him and let them do the one-on-one teaching. Greg Davis ran his offense for 13 seasons and called the plays, and Brown kept final say over every call . "I hear every play," Brown said. He knew he was a capable CEO. He also knew other coaches were better suited to certain jobs.

It worked. Texas won at least 10 games every year from 2001 through 2009 . Brown won the 2005 national title and was one Colt McCoy injury away from a second. For those nine seasons, 10 wins was the floor. In the 12 seasons since Brown left, Texas has gotten there four times .

The end wasn't pretty. Texas went 5-7 in 2010 and never won more than nine games again under Brown. Texas still jumped the gun. It went shopping before it knew what it was shopping for, and it hasn't stopped.

Texas is like nowhere else in the country — the coaches, the fans, the expectations, the donors, the money. The athletic director who hired Strong was fired less than two years later , after a plane towed a "Patterson Must Go" banner over the stadium. Herman won his last game at Texas, a bowl blowout, and was fired four days later , three weeks after his athletic director said publicly that Herman was the coach . During the fight over "The Eyes of Texas," a donor held up a $1 million pledge until the university decided whether to keep the song. Every coach since Brown has been hired to fix a scoreboard problem and then judged on everything else.

The money has only gotten bigger. Texas spent $375.9 million on athletics in fiscal 2025 , and the people who want a say now help pay for the roster. Managing those relationships is part of building the roster.

Sarkisian has put more of those BBs back in the box than anyone since Brown. After a 5-7 first season, he won the Big 12 in 2023, reached two straight playoff semifinals and strung together three straight 10-win seasons . Texas rewarded him with a contract that runs through the 2031 season . His reputation with quarterbacks is real. Arch Manning was praising Sarkisian's quarterback coaching more than a year before he committed to Texas. Quinn Ewers grew up wanting to be a Longhorn , backed out of his commitment to Herman's Texas and came home after Sarkisian took over .

That reputation helped bring those quarterbacks to Texas. Giving up the play sheet would mean handing over the work that built it.

Sarkisian has already shown he can run a unit from above it. Last season his defense ranked 40th nationally in yards allowed per game . Before the bowl game, he replaced his defensive coordinator and brought back Will Muschamp, Brown's defensive coordinator the last time Texas played for a national title. Through October 21, with six games played, Texas ranked second in the country in yards allowed per play . The offense Sarkisian calls ranked 103rd in yards per play .

Herman had the same decision to make. After the 2019 season, he gave up calling plays and said, "I needed to be a better head coach, which necessitated a play-caller on offense." Texas fired him a year later anyway . Ryan Day handed his play sheet to Chip Kelly at Ohio State in 2024. "As you move up, you've got to give up," Day said. Ohio State won the national title .

Sarkisian has been asked twice, a year apart, whether he would do the same. "No, because that's why I got hired," he said last October. "I was a really good offensive coordinator." After Oklahoma this month, he said, "Not a chance."

In 2013, Texas wanted Nick Saban. Seven years later, Saban won a national title with an offense he didn't call . He handed it to Steve Sarkisian.

Sarkisian says calling plays is why Texas hired him . He might be right. But only time will tell if that's the best thing at the end of the day for Texas' Fight(ing) chances moving forward.

articles.title: Cheap Android phones found with malware already installed
articles.summary: The Midnight Mimosa malware campaign hides inside cheap Android phone firmware, giving attackers powerful access before owners even turn devices on.
articles.body: Buying a cheap smartphone can feel like a smart move. After all, why spend hundreds more when a phone promises a big screen, decent cameras and all the Android apps you use every day? But what if that bargain phone came with a hidden surprise that was already hiding inside the device when you bought it? Security researchers at Bitdefender have uncovered a malware campaign called Midnight Mimosa that infects certain low-cost Android devices before their owners even turn them on. The malicious software hides inside the phone's firmware, giving attackers powerful access that ordinary apps never receive. Even more concerning, researchers found related malicious apps on Google Play. And this problem has reached the United States. ANDROID MALWARE CAN STEAL YOUR PIN AND BANK LOGINS Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET/ 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Android malware that comes installed from the factory Most smartphone security advice starts with being careful about what you download. That makes sense when a malicious app tricks you into installing it. Midnight Mimosa changes that equation because the infection can arrive with the phone itself. According to Bitdefender's investigation, the malware was discovered on low-cost, multi-brand Android devices built around MediaTek chipsets. Researchers found malicious applications embedded in the system software, where they could operate with elevated privileges. These privileges allow the malware to install additional apps without permission, remove existing applications and grant sensitive access to other software. It can also download and execute new code from remote servers. The researchers identified several versions hiding behind innocent-looking Android package names, including com.android.system.lite, com.android.sys.prot and com.android.sys.gmsprot. To most phone owners, those names would look like technical components that belong there. That's exactly what makes the scheme so difficult to spot. And because the malicious software lives in the system partition, a normal uninstall won't remove the underlying infection. Thousands of Android phones affected worldwide Bitdefender says it observed Midnight Mimosa on thousands of unique devices across more than 150 countries over approximately two years. Mexico, France and Italy had the highest observed numbers, followed by the United States, Germany, Brazil and Spain. Researchers also observed infected devices reporting model names associated with Doogee's S200 X and Cubot's KINGKONG X. However, the findings do not establish that every phone sold under those names is affected. Some devices in the campaign use misleading or counterfeit model identifiers, making it difficult to identify infections based on a phone's reported name alone. Another part of the investigation uncovered devices pretending to be expensive smartphones. Some reported names resembling Samsung Galaxy flagship models, while others imitated Apple's iPhone naming. In other words, a phone advertised as a premium Samsung or Apple device might actually contain inexpensive Android hardware running modified software. Researchers found that some counterfeit devices even reported legitimate looking Samsung model identifiers. That makes checking the model name alone an unreliable way to confirm authenticity. The investigation also identified firmware signed with certificates associated with Shenzhen Zediel, a Chinese device manufacturer. However, Bitdefender emphasized that this does not establish that the company created the malware or knew about its presence. Exactly where the malicious code entered the manufacturing and distribution process remains unknown. What the hidden Android malware actually does You might expect malware this powerful to steal passwords immediately or display obvious warnings. Instead, Midnight Mimosa appears primarily designed to generate money for its operators while staying out of sight. One way it earns money is through advertising fraud. The malicious system component silently installs apps that look like weather tools, app lockers and other everyday utilities. Those apps can display legitimate advertisements in hidden windows or generate clicks without the owner touching the screen. Advertisers may end up paying for activity that never came from a real person. Bitdefender identified at least 32 unique disguised applications involved in the broader operation. The malware can also repeatedly install and remove these apps, making them harder to notice during a casual check of the phone. Your phone could become part of a botnet The advertising fraud is only part of the story. Researchers also discovered software that can turn infected phones into residential proxy servers. Here's what that means. Someone operating the malware could route internet traffic through your phone's connection. To websites and online services, that traffic may appear to come from your home or mobile network rather than the person actually controlling it. Such connections can be valuable to cybercriminals because they help conceal where online activity originates. The same infrastructure could potentially support larger botnet operations or distributed denial-of-service attacks. Bitdefender confirmed that the malware contained the technology needed to turn infected phones into residential proxy servers. However, the researchers later clarified that one server they reached was actually a sinkhole, a system used to intercept malicious communications. Their testing did not demonstrate active traffic being relayed through the infected device. The underlying capability remains concerning because it could allow operators to route traffic through a phone owner's connection. AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION The malware can temporarily disable Google Play One particularly troubling finding involves how Midnight Mimosa avoids security checks. Before installing certain malicious apps, Midnight Mimosa temporarily disables the Google Play Store app. Bitdefender believes this helps the malware avoid detection by Google Play Protect during installation. Once the process finishes, the malware re-enables the Store, reducing the chances that the phone owner will notice anything unusual. The process happens without the phone owner's involvement. Some versions also manipulate Android's installer records to make applications appear to have come from Google Play, even when the malware installed them directly. So a quick look at where an app supposedly originated may not tell the whole story. Here are the 13 apps identified in the investigation Wavrge, App Icon DIY, Audify, QR Pocket, All Deleted Messages Recovery, WeatherGo, CoolWeather, Daily Weather, Lock & Hide, QuickText Extractor, NoteMaster, Tap to Translate and Tasky. These apps offered functions such as weather forecasts, QR scanning, message recovery and audio editing. However, researchers found that they could also generate unwanted advertising activity, including displaying ads outside their normal interfaces. Unlike the malware embedded in phone firmware, these Google Play apps lacked the elevated system privileges needed to silently install other applications. The apps were associated with 13 different signing certificates and at least two developer accounts, identified as fivedev and CPS Developer. Are these apps still on Google Play? Checks of the Google Play listings for all 13 apps found that none were available for download. However, it remains unclear whether Google removed the apps or their developers withdrew them. CyberGuy reached out to Google for comment but did not receive a response before our deadline. What should you do if you recognize one? Check your Android phone's installed apps. If you find one of these applications, verify that its package identifier matches the one listed in Bitdefender's report before uninstalling it. Different apps can share similar names. Even when an app disappears from Google Play, it can remain installed on your phone. The findings show why downloading an app from an official store doesn't automatically guarantee its safety. Phone owners reported malware returning after removal The findings also connect with complaints posted by some Doogee and Cubot smartphone owners on the XDA forums. Users described suspicious system applications that reappeared after attempts to remove them. One Doogee Fire 3 Max owner reported that an official firmware update introduced the infection. According to that account, reverting to an older firmware version removed the problem, while reinstalling the newer update brought it back. Other forum participants reported that subsequent firmware updates resolved their infections. However, Bitdefender identified one of the suspicious packages discussed in the forum, com.android.non.szcz, as belonging to the same malware family. That creates a frustrating situation for owners. A software update is normally something I encourage people to install for better security. But when the firmware itself is compromised, the source and integrity of the update become especially important. How to protect your Android phone from preinstalled malware The most effective protection starts before you buy a device. However, there are useful precautions if you already own an inexpensive Android phone or suspect something unusual is happening. 1. Buy from reputable sellers and verify the phone Be especially careful with unusually cheap smartphones advertised as premium models. Counterfeit devices can copy familiar names and appearances while using entirely different hardware. Choose established retailers and authorized sellers when possible. Check the manufacturer's official website to confirm that the model exists and matches the advertised specifications. An extremely low price deserves a closer look, especially when the seller provides limited information about software updates or warranty support. ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK 2. Check whether your Android phone is certified by Google Before trusting an unfamiliar Android phone, check whether Google recognizes it as a certified device. Play Protect certification indicates that a device has met Google's compatibility requirements. However, certification alone cannot guarantee that its firmware is free of malware. Here's how to check: If your phone says Device is not certified, contact the manufacturer or seller to investigate. An uncertified device does not automatically mean it contains malware, but it deserves additional scrutiny. 3. Keep Google Play Protect enabled Google Play Protect is Android's built-in malware protection. It scans apps for harmful behavior and can warn you about or remove known threats. However, it is not 100% effective at detecting every malicious app, especially malware hidden deep within a phone's system software. To check it, open the Google Play Store > your profile picture > Play Protect > Settings. Make sure Scan apps with Play Protect is enabled. Then return to the Play Protect screen to check for harmful apps. A clean scan is reassuring, but it does not guarantee your phone is free of malware, particularly if the infection is embedded in its firmware. That's why we also recommend strong antivirus software as an additional layer of protection. 4. Use strong antivirus protection Strong antivirus software adds another layer of protection by monitoring suspicious behavior and detecting threats that may go unnoticed. In fact, Bitdefender's investigation began when its behavioral detection technology flagged an unusual system component. This shows why monitoring how apps behave can help uncover threats that traditional scans might miss. However, even strong antivirus software may detect malicious firmware without having the permissions needed to remove it. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 5. Review installed apps and sensitive permissions Open Settings > Apps > See all apps or the equivalent app list on your Android device. Look for applications you don't recognize, especially ones requesting unusual access. Next, review Settings > Security & privacy > Privacy controls > Permission manager, where available. Check permissions such as SMS access and other sensitive capabilities. Accessibility and notification access may have their own settings pages. Menu names vary by manufacturer and Android version. Be cautious about unfamiliar apps with extensive permissions. However, don't randomly disable legitimate Android system components because their technical names look strange. 6. Watch for unusual phone behavior An infected phone may show signs such as unexplained mobile data usage, excessive background activity, unexpected advertisements or apps appearing without your permission. Check Settings > Network & internet > SIMs > App data usage, or your manufacturer's equivalent, to investigate unusual data consumption. These symptoms can have harmless explanations, and Midnight Mimosa may operate without obvious warning signs. Treat unexpected activity as a reason to investigate rather than proof of infection. 7. Be careful with firmware updates and factory resets Install updates supplied through your manufacturer's verified support channels. However, if you suspect the device firmware itself is infected, contact the manufacturer before attempting a repair. A factory reset generally removes personal data and user-installed apps. It does not necessarily replace compromised software stored in the system partition. Bitdefender says removing Midnight Mimosa's privileged component may require firmware-level cleanup or specialized tools such as Android Debug Bridge. For most people, manually modifying system firmware introduces additional risks. If the manufacturer cannot provide a verified clean firmware image, replacing the device may be the safest practical option. 8. Secure important accounts if you suspect an infection If you believe your phone has been compromised, use a separate trusted device to change important passwords, starting with your primary email and financial accounts. Review recent account activity and enable multifactor authentication where available. Consider using an authenticator app or passkeys on a trusted device rather than relying exclusively on SMS codes. Bitdefender identified sensitive capabilities in the malware, including potential access to notifications and SMS messages. The researchers did not observe every capability being actively exploited, so account compromise should not be assumed without evidence. Nevertheless, protecting important accounts is a sensible precaution when you can no longer trust the phone's operating system. Kurt's key takeaways I've always liked the idea of getting more for less, especially when it comes to technology. You shouldn't have to spend flagship phone money to get a device that works reliably. But this investigation exposes a problem that deserves far more attention from the companies making and selling inexpensive smartphones. When malware arrives embedded in the firmware, the owner has very little control. You can be careful about downloads, check permissions and follow security advice, yet still end up with a compromised device straight out of the box. What concerns me most is the possibility that your phone could be quietly earning money for someone else while using a connection you pay for. And if removing the infection requires specialized firmware work, the burden lands on the person who bought the device. Manufacturers and marketplaces need to take greater responsibility for verifying the software that ships on the products they sell. A low price should never mean accepting hidden software that puts your privacy and security at risk. Would you pay more for a smartphone from a manufacturer you trust, or do you think companies selling budget phones should be held legally responsible when malware comes preinstalled? articles.summary: McBee Dynasty star Steven McBee Sr. has agreed to pay more than $7.18 million to the US government after settling his federal crop fraud case.
articles.body: McBee Dynasty star Steven McBee Sr. has agreed to pay more than $7.18 million to the US government after settling his federal crop fraud case. The reality TV personality, 54, must pay a forfeiture judgment of $3,158,923 and restitution of $4,022,124 to the United States Department of Agriculture, according to court documents filed by the US Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri and obtained by Us Weekly on Thursday, October 22.Under the settlement, McBee must pay $300,000 within 14 days of the agreement’s effective date. He is required to pay the remaining balance within 10 months.The settlement comes weeks after McBee was released from prison in September, having served approximately nine months at the Federal Prison Camp in Yankton, South Dakota. He will complete the remainder of his 24-month sentence under supervised release.Steven McBee Sr. returns to family farm after prison releaseFollowing his release, the McBee Farm & Cattle Co. founder took to Instagram to share a glimpse of his return to family life at his farm in Gallatin, Missouri.“A little more appreciation for the simple things in life....Thank you Lord for all the blessings in my life,” he wrote on September 12, alongside a video of his return.His son, Steven McBee Jr., responded to the post, expressing happiness at having his father back home.“Best 24 hours we've had in a long, long time. So many good memories to make and time to have together as a COMPLETE family!” he commented.Days after his release, Steven Sr. also shared a look at a newly renovated office that his family had prepared as a surprise while he was away.“So I thought I'd just show you guys my new office,” he said in an Instagram video, expressing gratitude to his family for the renovation, which included new furniture and a coffee bar.“I'm just so fortunate and blessed to have the people in my life that I do,” he added, saying he had already been making extensive use of the space.Why was Steven McBee Sr. sentenced to prison?The US Department of Justice announced in November 2024 that McBee had pleaded guilty to a multi-million-dollar fraud scheme involving federal crop insurance benefits he was not entitled to receive.According to the department, McBee admitted that in 2018 he sold more than 1.2 million bushels of corn and nearly 416,000 bushels of soybeans to another party as part of the scheme.Although he faced a potential sentence of up to 30 years in federal prison, a judge sentenced him to two years behind bars in October 2025. He surrendered to the Federal Prison Camp in Yankton in December 2025.McBee’s September release came after he served approximately nine months in custody. He will now serve the remainder of his sentence under supervised release, according to the information provided.Steven McBee Jr. spoke about his father’s time behind barsIn July, Steven McBee Jr., 33, spoke exclusively to Us Weekly about how his father was coping with his time in prison and the family’s anticipation of his return.“Thankfully, we're down to less than two months now before he gets out,” Steven Jr. said at the time, explaining that his father had been able to enter a programme that allowed him to reduce his time in custody.He also said his father was expected to spend four to six months under home confinement after his release.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. articles.title: Soundcore’s latest noise-crushing headphones are on sale for a new low price
articles.summary: The Space 2 have fallen to $106, their lowest price to date, at multiple retailers. Unsurprisingly, they offer improved ANC and sound over the first-gen model.
articles.body: My colleague John Higgins considered Soundcore’s Space One some of the best budget noise-canceling headphones you could buy when they launched in 2023 — and their successor has only improved upon their winning formula, albeit with a $30 price increase. Thankfully, the Soundcore Space 2 are currently on sale at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart in all three colors for an all-time low of $106.49 ($23 off), making them even easier to recommend. [Product: Soundcore Space 2 | The Space 2 builds on the original with improved active noise cancellation, particularly when it comes to the low-frequency sounds associated with trains and airplane engines. They also deliver more accurate sound performance thanks to various design upgrades, while retaining many of the same features that made the Sound One sound so good for the price, including support for high-resolution LDAC audio. You also still get access to HearID 3.0, which lets you personalize the sound by listening to a series of samples and adjusting accordingly. Battery life is another welcome improvement. The Space 2 can last up to 50 hours with ANC enabled or 70 hours with it switched off, up from 40 and 55 hours, respectively, on the original. And when your battery dies, you can still use the equipped 3.5mm jack for wired listening. They’ll also automatically pause playback when you take them off, which is handy when you need to step away without losing your place in a song or podcast.

articles.title: Hottest toy for Christmas? Nvidia CEO plays with adorable Microduck robots, 20,000 sell | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a "nap," and summersaulted on voice command.
articles.body:
Earlier this week, a video of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang playing with a flock of waddling Microducks during his keynote at the company’s GTC Berlin conference went viral. The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a “nap,” and summersaulted on voice command. They were so darn cute that by the next day, preorders of the Microducks surpassed 20,000 units, Hugging Face’s Clem Delangue said in a tweet.

The Microducks are expected to be delivered in time for Christmas, meaning these robots might already be on their way to becoming the hottest toy for the holiday season. Delangue thinks they might end up being the best-selling robot of the year, and possibly not even for kids. The promotional videos show adults playing with them , too.

Microducks are open source devices produced by Pollen Robotics, a company acquired by Hugging Face in 2025, which means they are now an Nvidia company. The GPU giant bought Hugging Face in September. This is actually Hugging Face’s second robot, after the also-cute Reachy Mini.

Microducks were trained using Nvidia’s technology stack, wherein simulations of them were taught basic tricks (walk, sit, stand, etc.) that they ship with. Pollen says that owners can train their robots with new tricks and then share them with the community.

Here’s the video below. Enjoy it as a palate cleanser after the scary black eye the AI industry gave itself this week , as AI involvement was blamed for cyberattack after cyberattack. OK, AI might seriously damage the world. But it can be fun, too. It’s hard to watch this video without ordering one.

articles.title: AOORA on singing Indian and Korean national anthems: It was a deeply personal honour
articles.summary: Singing the national anthems of India and South Korea at the Republic of Korea’s National Day Reception in Mumbai was a moment of pride and honour for
articles.body: Singing the national anthems of India and South Korea at the Republic of Korea’s National Day Reception in Mumbai was a moment of pride and honour for South Korean singer AOORA. The performance was deeply personal for the artiste, whose Korean roots remain central to his identity, while the warmth he has received in India has fostered a bond that goes beyond music and has made the country an integral part of his life.Hosted by the Consulate General of the Republic of Korea, the reception took place at the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel on October 23. AOORA was invited to perform at the event, which celebrated the friendship between the two countries. Among those present were Rajesh Gawande, Chief of Protocol, Government of Maharashtra, and Dongwan Yoo, Consul General of the Republic of Korea, along with diplomats and industrialists.Reflecting on the experience, AOORA says, “The two anthems have different languages, melodies and expressions, but both carry a deep love for one’s country. For me, one holds the familiarity of growing up in Korea, while the other reflects a connection I have built with India. I wanted to honour the individual spirit of each. After I finished, I felt a mixture of relief, pride and gratitude. Two very important parts of my life had come together on one stage. It is a moment I will carry with me.”For AOORA, the performance also brought into focus the place both countries hold in his life. He adds, “Korea is my birthplace, and India has become my second home. One connects me to my roots, and the other reminds me of the love and acceptance I have received here. I wanted to sing each with sincerity and respect.”AOORA on Bollywood, India and Korea’s cultural tiesAOORA has often spoken about his affection for India. In a previous interaction with us, he shared, “I find India and Indians beautiful, and I connect with this country really well. The warmth I’ve experienced in India makes me feel good. India as a country has been incredibly therapeutic for me. It’s a place where the soul finds comfort amidst the chaos.”The singer first came into the limelight in India with his rendition of Bappi Lahiri’s Jimmy Jimmy (Disco Dancer, 1982) and has since been known for dancing to popular Bollywood songs. Recalling what draws him to Bollywood music and dance, he said, “Last summer, I saw a video of the song, Cham Cham (Baaghi, 2016), and found it vibrant and aligning with my style. I resonated with the idea of so many people coming together to sing and dance in the video. I feel Bollywood films reflect society and what’s happening in people’s lives. In India, I have witnessed the same flavour during Navratri and Diwali.”Beyond his love for Indian music and festivities, AOORA hopes to strengthen cultural ties between the two countries. The K-pop singer and songwriter said, “There are so many striking similarities between these two countries, and I want to bring them closer, culturally. That’s my goal. When I see people back home unaware of the real India, I try to tell them more. I want people in Korea to experience the warmth and love that I have got here.”Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
articles.summary: Apple is expected to finally launch a touchscreen MacBook Pro. Windows laptops have had them for ages, and this Lenovo Yoga 9n RTX Spark has some features worth copying.
articles.body: It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook. Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs. The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse. [Image: 2-in-1s can be seen as a weird compromise between laptops and tablets. I just think they’re neat. The Yoga 9n’s included stylus works for note-taking and drawing on its excellent OLED display, but you can also use it on the haptic trackpad for a Wacom-like experience, without blocking the screen with your hand. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Lenovo’s stylus relies on USB-C charging, which is fine, but not as convenient as always having it charged and ready to go while attached to your laptop. [Image: [Image: I don’t expect Apple to make a standard convertible laptop after all this time. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky. My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. The HomeView’s lack of apps is perplexing. The iPhone Duo is a little messy. Current MacBooks are so great, it’s easy to forget the butterfly keyboard fiasco wasn’t all that long ago. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it. Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: 'SNL' Weekend Update anchor calls Republicans slurs, mocks Charlie Kirk in stand-up special
articles.summary: Michael Che's Netflix special opens with jokes about Charlie Kirk's killing and repeatedly uses the R-word to mock President Donald Trump and MAGA supporters.
articles.body: "Saturday Night Live" Weekend Update co-anchor Michael Che joked about Charlie Kirk's killing and repeatedly used the R-word while mocking President Donald Trump and his supporters in his new Netflix special, "Michael Che: Shot in Minnesota." The new stand-up special was taped at the First Avenue music venue in Minneapolis. Che opened the show by saying he felt so good that he might get emotional."I feel like Erika Kirk on this stage. That’s no disrespect to the Kirks, by the way." Che said he didn't know who Charlie Kirk was before the activist was killed, joking that he initially thought people were talking about "the dude from Star Trek." A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH "I was like, 'What? They shot Captain Kirk?'"Che said he then watched the graphic video of Charlie Kirk's assassination to better understand what happened, saying, "I wish I did not see that s---." "I don’t know if you saw," he told his audience, "but it’s f---ed up." Che said the best explanation he had heard for why Kirk was killed was that "in this country, straight White Christian conservative men are being silenced." He recalled having a debate about the issue "with this r-----ed guy." "I know you shouldn’t use that word, but, I do ... It’s because I still see them. I’ll stop saying it when I stop seeing it," he said. He further defended his use of the slur, saying, "Ever since we stopped using the word 'r-----ed,' r-----ed people have taken over the world. I don’t think that s--- is a coincidence." HASAN PIKER DEFENDS USING INCENDIARY TERMS LIKE 'INBRED' OR 'ZIONIST PIG' AGAINST OPPONENTS Che said that if people still used the R-word, Trump never could have become president. "He just kept getting stronger and stronger. Now, we can’t stop him ... I watched those debates. They never know what the f--- to say to that guy. They don’t got the language ... 'He’s unpresidential.' It’s like, 'No, he’s a r-----ed guy.'" Che said the Minneapolis audience would know exactly what he was talking about, because every time he turns on the news, "Minnesota is fighting some group of r-----s." "No, it’s important to say it. R-----ed meaning regressive. Bunch of motherf---ers trying to take all our rights away." Che also called Trump a "r----- whisperer." "That’s all politics is these days. Just r----- whispering." He mocked Trump’s ability to appeal to supporters through red MAGA hats and simple messaging, attributing the popularity of the recognizable caps to the fact that "r-----ed guys love hats." BROADCAST BIAS: FEMINIST FREAKOUT OVER SHANE GILLIS COMMENT IS THE REAL JOKE The 'SNL' co-anchor said the president would have made a great kindergarten teacher because he knows how to talk to people who "don’t like to think that much." Che argued Americans do not take presidential politics seriously enough, suggesting that the country should have a list of potential candidates years in advance. "If it’s the most important job in the free world, we still don’t know? There’s no list?" he joked. "Right now, ESPN has a list of the top 500 high school quarterbacks in the country. But every four years, we end up in this f---ed up 'Would You Rather.' "One n----- is 80, the other n----- is 80-er." Che later shifted into personal material about aging, drinking, relationships, sex and fatherhood, closing by imagining God as an absent parent. "I think God loves us. I think he just had us at a very young age. He realized he had more living to do. 'I gotta get the f--- out of here. Here, take this book. I’ll be right back.' I ain’t seen him since."
